title: Tile Pop
statement: A rail holds a row of tiles whose weights are given in weights. Two tiles that are currently next to each other can be popped together when their weights differ by at most tolerance. After a pop the tiles on either side close the gap and become neighbours. You may pop as many pairs as you like, in any order, or stop at any moment. Your score is the total weight of all tiles that were popped. Return the maximum score.

examples.explanation: Pop 9 and 8 (they differ by 1). Then 6 and 5 are neighbours, so pop them. Now 4 and 2 are neighbours and differ by 2, so pop them too. Every tile is popped, for a score of 4 + 6 + 5 + 9 + 8 + 2 = 34.
No two neighbouring tiles differ by 5 or less, so nothing can be popped and the score is 0.

hints.content: Look at the leftmost tile of a stretch of the rail. Either it is never popped, or it is popped together with exactly one partner. What has to be true of everything between them?
Everything strictly between two tiles that pop together must have been popped away before they become neighbours, so pairs never cross each other: they either nest or sit side by side.
For a stretch from i to j, define clear(i, j) as whether all its tiles can be popped, and best(i, j) as the highest score using only tiles i to j. Only stretches of even length can be cleared.

For best(i, j): leave tile i unpopped and take best(i + 1, j), or pair i with a tile k whose weight is within tolerance, where clear(i + 1, k - 1) holds, and add the weights of tiles i to k plus best(k + 1, j).
clear(i, j) is true when some valid k also has clear(k + 1, j). Fill the table with i decreasing and j increasing: O(n^3) time, O(n^2) space. Trying every pop order directly is exponential.

testCases.explanation: Nested pops clear the whole rail.
A single tile has no partner.
Exact matches popped from the inside out: 7 and 7, then 5 and 5, then 3 and 3.
Equal tiles are never neighbours and cannot be made so, so nothing pops.
Two pairs of neighbours that differ by 1.
The tile of 100 pops with nothing. The two 9s pop first, which makes 5 and 6 neighbours, so they pop too.
A 60-tile rail where every pair is allowed: exhaustive search tries a huge number of pop orders.
The largest rail with a moderate tolerance.
The largest rail where every pair is allowed, so every tile pops.

solutions.title: Try every pop in every order
solutions.intuition: Simulate the rail: at each step choose any legal neighbouring pair, pop it, and recurse on the shorter rail.
solutions.approach: play(rail, gained) tries every adjacent pair within tolerance, removes it, and recurses with the gain increased by the pair's weights. The answer is the largest gained value seen, including stopping at once.
solutions.pseudocode:
play(rail, gained): top = gained
  for i in 0..len-2: if |rail[i] - rail[i+1]| <= tolerance:
    top = max(top, play(rail without i and i+1, gained + rail[i] + rail[i+1]))
  return top
solutions.timeComplexity: Exponential: the number of pop sequences grows faster than 2^(n/2)
solutions.spaceComplexity: O(n^2) for the copied rails along the recursion
commonMistakes: Forgetting that stopping is allowed, so the best score may be less than the total weight.
Letting tiles that are not currently adjacent pop together.
solutions.interviewExplanation: Simulating the story is the safest way to be sure of the rules and works for about twenty tiles. The same sub-rail arises from many different pop orders, which signals overlapping subproblems and leads to the interval DP.

steps.title: First pop
steps.content: In [4, 6, 5, 9, 8, 2] with tolerance 2, popping 9 and 8 leaves [4, 6, 5, 2] with 17 gained.

steps.title: Finish
steps.content: Popping 6 and 5, then 4 and 2, gains 11 and 6 more, ending at 34, the sum of all tiles.

solutions.title: Interval DP over stretches of the rail
solutions.intuition: Popped tiles form non-crossing pairs, and everything inside a pair is popped first, so a stretch's answer is built from smaller stretches.
solutions.approach: Let clear[i][j] say stretch i..j can be fully popped and best[i][j] be its best score. Both come from the leftmost tile i: either best skips it (best[i+1][j]), or i pairs with a k (k - i odd) with |w[i] - w[k]| <= tolerance and clear[i+1][k-1], giving sum(i..k) + best[k+1][j]; clear[i][j] holds if such a k also has clear[k+1][j]. Empty stretches are clear with score 0.
solutions.timeComplexity: O(n^3): roughly n^3 / 12, about 670,000 inner steps at n = 200
commonMistakes: Requiring the whole stretch to be cleared for best, which forbids leaving tiles behind.
Allowing k with an even gap, which leaves an odd number of tiles inside that can never be fully popped.
Forgetting the empty-stretch base cases for clear[i+1][i] and best[n][*].
solutions.interviewExplanation: A popped pair (i, k) requires the tiles between them to be gone first, and they must pair among themselves, so pairs nest or sit side by side but never cross. That is a classic interval DP: the state is a stretch, and the transition chooses the partner of its leftmost tile. Two tables are needed because 'can this stretch be emptied' is a different question from 'how much can I score in it'. The cubic cost comes from the choice of k.

steps.title: Small stretches
steps.content: For the first example, tiles 9 and 8 (indices 3, 4) are clear with best 17, and 6 and 5 (indices 1, 2) are clear with best 11.

steps.title: Combine
steps.content: The tiles of weight 4 and 2 (indices 0 and 5) differ by 2 and enclose the cleared stretch of indices 1 to 4, so clear[0][5] is true and best[0][5] = 34.
